name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS_12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q01 - Properties and reactions of organometallic Grignard reagents and alkyl halides

questiontext.text:
Given below are four statements:

Statement I: Grignard reagents (\(\mathrm{RMgX}\)) are synthesized by reacting alkyl or aryl halides with magnesium metal in dry ether solvent.

Statement II: In Grignard reagents, the carbon–magnesium bond is covalent and completely non-polar.

Statement III: Grignard reagents react rapidly with any proton donor, including water and alcohols, to yield the corresponding hydrocarbons.

Statement IV: Alkyl halides react with metallic sodium in dry ether to form symmetrical alkanes containing double the number of carbon atoms present in the alkyl halide.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Organometallic compounds contain carbon–metal bonds. In Grignard reagents (\(\mathrm{RMgX}\)), carbon is directly bonded to electropositive magnesium, rendering the carbon center nucleophilic and basic. Haloalkanes also undergo coupling reactions with sodium metal (Wurtz reaction) to construct carbon–carbon single bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Synthesis in Anhydrous Medium
Alkyl halides (\(\mathrm{RX}\)) react smoothly with magnesium metal turnings in anhydrous diethyl ether to produce alkylmagnesium halides (\(\mathrm{RMgX}\)). Anhydrous conditions are essential to prevent premature decomposition of the reagent. This confirms the validity of the synthesis proposition.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Nature of the Carbon–Magnesium Bond
Magnesium has an electronegativity of approximately \(1.2\) whereas carbon has an electronegativity of approximately \(2.5\). Because of this marked electronegativity difference, the carbon–magnesium covalent bond is highly polarized, with a partial negative charge residing on carbon and a partial positive charge on magnesium: \(\mathrm{R}^{\delta-}–\mathrm{Mg}^{\delta+}\mathrm{X}\). The magnesium–halogen bond is predominantly ionic. Describing the carbon–magnesium linkage as non-polar contradicts its strongly polar nature.

Step 4: Evaluation of Reactivity Toward Proton Donors
Because the carbanionic carbon in \(\mathrm{RMgX}\) acts as a potent Brønsted base, it abstracts protons vigorously from water, alcohols, amines, or other acidic hydrogen sources to produce the parent alkane according to \(\mathrm{RMgX} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{RH} + \mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\). This confirms the high reactivity toward protic species.

Step 5: Evaluation of Coupling with Sodium Metal
The reaction of two moles of an alkyl halide with sodium metal in dry ether yields an alkane containing twice the number of carbon atoms: \(2\mathrm{RX} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{R–R} + 2\mathrm{NaX}\). This process is recognized as the Wurtz reaction and provides symmetrical alkanes.

Step 6: Synthesis and Final Conclusion
The principles governing preparation in dry ether, protonolysis to alkanes, and sodium-mediated Wurtz coupling are scientifically accurate, whereas attributing non-polarity to the carbon–magnesium bond is scientifically incorrect. Therefore, the valid proposition corresponds to the selection where the first, third, and fourth statements are correct while the second statement is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I, III and IV only are correct
Statements I, II and IV only are correct
Statements II and III only are correct
Statements I, II, III and IV are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CLASS_12_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_STATEMENT_BASED_4_Q02 - Chirality stereochemical principles and substitution reaction mechanisms

questiontext.text:
Given below are four statements:

Statement I: An optically active organic compound that rotates the plane of plane-polarised light in a clockwise direction is termed dextrorotatory and is designated by a positive \((+)\) sign.

Statement II: A carbon atom bonded to four distinct atoms or groups lacks reflection symmetry and is referred to as an asymmetric carbon or stereocentre.

Statement III: Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) at a chiral carbon center of an optically active haloalkane proceeds with complete retention of configuration.

Statement IV: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers exhibits zero net optical rotation due to external compensation and is called a racemic mixture.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Optical activity arises from molecular asymmetry or chirality. The interaction of chiral molecules with plane-polarised light leads to optical rotation. In nucleophilic substitution, the stereochemical trajectory of attack dictates whether configuration is inverted, retained, or racemized.

Step 2: Evaluation of Optical Rotation Conventions
Substances that rotate the oscillation plane of plane-polarised light to the right (clockwise) as viewed looking toward the light source are termed dextrorotatory (from the Latin dexter, meaning right). This direction of optical rotation is denoted by placing a plus sign \((+)\) or the prefix d- before the name of the substance.

Step 3: Evaluation of Asymmetric Centers and Chirality
When all four valencies of an \(sp^3\)-hybridized carbon atom are satisfied by four structurally different substituents, that carbon atom is described as an asymmetric carbon or chiral center (stereocentre). A molecule containing a single asymmetric carbon atom lacks planes or centers of symmetry, making its spatial structure non-superimposable on its mirror image.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Stereochemical Course of the Substitution Reaction
In an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction, the incoming nucleophile attacks the substrate from the side directly opposite to the departing halide leaving group (backside attack). As the carbon–nucleophile bond develops simultaneously with the cleavage of the carbon–leaving group bond, the remaining three groups attached to the central carbon invert like an umbrella turned inside-out in a strong gale. Consequently, an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) process at a chiral center proceeds with complete inversion of spatial configuration (Walden inversion), not retention.

Step 5: Evaluation of Racemic Modifications and Enantiomeric Pairs
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light by exactly equal magnitudes but in opposite directions. In an equimolar (\(1:1\)) mixture of two enantiomers, the dextrorotation caused by one enantiomer is precisely cancelled by the levorotation caused by the other. This phenomenon is known as external compensation, rendering the racemic mixture \((±)\) completely optically inactive.

Step 6: Synthesis and Final Conclusion
The explanations describing dextrorotatory classification, the definition of asymmetric stereocentres, and the optical inactivity of racemic mixtures are scientifically valid. In contrast, stating that bimolecular nucleophilic substitution yields retention of configuration is erroneous because backside attack enforces stereochemical inversion. Hence, the correct combination identifies the first, second, and fourth statements as valid and the third statement as invalid.

answer.text: Statements I, II and III only are correct
Statements I, II and IV only are correct
Statements II, III and IV only are correct
Statements I, III and IV only are correct
